items.title: Measuring Users' Security and Privacy Concerns About Third-Party Community Bots on Discord
items.abstract: Third-party community-based bots are central to how social platforms such as Discord work. They moderate content, manage roles, play music, and support AI-assisted conversations across millions of servers. Yet when a bot is installed in a server, it can access messages, user profiles, and server metadata concerning members who did not participate in the installation decision, with no standardized way to communicate the associated security and privacy implications. In this paper, we analyze 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews spanning 49 detected languages and five years of feedback (2021-2026). We employ LLM-based knowledge distillation and fine-tune a DeBERTa-based classifier to identify candidate security and privacy (S&P)-relevant reviews. After manually validating the complete classifier-positive set, we retain 8,832 reviews identified as S&P-relevant, representing an observed pipeline yield of 4.82%, and map them to a 31-theme S&P taxonomy extending prior work. Our results show that S&P-related reviews focus heavily on Data Sharing (30.5%) and Data Collection (16.2%). Confession and anonymity bots have pipeline-identified SPRRs above 50%, more than ten times the ecosystem-wide pipeline yield of 4.82%. Star ratings may obscure the frequency and valence of S&P-related discussion, while conventional metadata features, such as permission count and administrator status, show only weak associations with user-reported S&P concerns. We then build BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review-derived S&P signals with bot metadata to provide on-demand decision support for the community-based bot ecosystem. BotLens exposes six tools through a Model Context Protocol server, supporting bot-level checkups, server-wide comparison, and integration with AI agents.

items.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
items.abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

items.title: Meta Models: Models that Model Learning
items.abstract: Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.

items.title: Metabolic Cost of Transport in Walking in Middle-Aged Adults Using an Ankle Exoskeleton
items.abstract: This study evaluated energy expenditure while walking with a powered ankle exoskeleton in middle-aged adults. Participants wore a bilateral ankle exoskeleton. Metabolic cost was measured via indirect calorimetry. Participants walked on a treadmill without the exoskeleton and with the exoskeleton unpowered, powered, and unpowered again. Net metabolic cost of transport (MCOT) was calculated. Behaviors exhibited include a decrease in MCOT, an increase in MCOT, and initial changes that diminished with time. This variability may be explained by differences in adaptation times, which may be more pronounced among middle-aged adults due to age-related changes in gait and declines in neuromuscular and sensory function. These results underscore the importance of age-related considerations in training protocols, recognizing that middle-aged adults may require longer, more structured training than young adults. Insufficient adaptation may prevent users from experiencing metabolic improvements that could contribute to reduced injury risk and lower rates of musculoskeletal disorders.

items.title: Metacognition in the Era of Generative AI: Understanding Human Cognitive Engagement and AI Reliance
items.abstract: The growing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into human cognitive activities, including problem-solving, decision-making, learning and information processing, has raised important questions about cognitive work allocation, metacognitive control and independent performance. Although GenAI can enhance efficiency by reducing cognitive demands, excessive reliance may weaken users’ engagement in reasoning, verification and independent task execution. This review examines the relationship between GenAI use and human cognition, with particular emphasis on cognitive offloading, appropriate reliance, over-reliance, automation bias and independent performance. Drawing on existing research, it explores how the effects of cognitive offloading depend on task characteristics and the distribution of cognitive responsibility between users and AI systems. The review further considers interventions such as think-first strategies, cognitive forcing functions, reflection, verification prompts and adaptive scaffolding that aim to preserve human cognitive engagement while benefiting from AI assistance. In addition, it examines behavioural telemetry including prompt intent, interaction timing, response editing and verification activities as a potential means of identifying patterns of engagement and reliance during multi-turn human AI interactions. These observable behaviours are treated as indirect indicators rather than definitive measures of internal cognitive processes. The review highlights the importance of evaluating not only task performance with AI assistance but also users’ ability to perform independently when such assistance is unavailable. It identifies a need for integrated frameworks that connect cognitive work allocation, metacognition, observable interaction patterns, reliance calibration and independent performance over time. Such frameworks may support the development of human-centred GenAI systems that improve task effectiveness while maintaining users’ critical thinking, self-regulation and cognitive autonomy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Mitigating Cognitive Offloading in AI-Assisted Learning Through Structural Gamification
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) tutors remove exactly the effort that learning requires: students adopt the instant answer, offload the reasoning to the model, and retain less. Friction-based tutors reverse the offloading, yet learners disengage from unbounded friction. This paper tests whether game-structural mechanics—checkpoints, low-stakes failure with retry, and a rescue that guarantees completion—hold the learner inside a tutor's deliberate friction. In a multi-agent simulation of 180 students (three independent draws of 60) across six levels of seeded misconception burden, each student works the same ten-part physics problem under three tutor conditions: instant answer, strict Socratic, and a ten-checkpoint quest in which every part is unlocked only by the student's own attempt. The quest condition removes the measured offloading: students produce 0.999 of the solution steps against 0.302 under the instant answer, self-reported offloading is 1.48 versus 5.58 on a 6-point scale, and every student names the instant-answer condition as the one in which they offloaded most. Structuring the friction also removes its cost: quest sessions complete in 100 percent of cases, against a 14.4 percent abandonment rate in the strict condition, where sessions that run long end when the student's reported motivation reaches the floor. Both friction conditions raise the unaided posttest far above the shared pretest (0.928 and 0.885 versus 0.455); the instant-answer condition reaches only 0.563. Friction that is structured as bounded progression holds the learner inside productive struggle without the attrition that plain withholding carries.

items.title: Motivations for social value creation in commercial buildings: evidence from New Zealand
items.abstract: Social value creation is a stated priority in commercial property and ESG agendas, yet little is known about why owners and occupiers pursue social initiatives or what sustains them. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT) and its sub-theory of organismic integration, this study examines the motivations underpinning social value in Auckland's prime office market, New Zealand. Eleven semi-structured interviews with eighteen owners, occupiers and agents across ten organisations were analysed thematically alongside corporate sustainability reporting. Motivations cluster around four drivers: market obligations, environmental imperatives, employee priorities and socio-cultural responsibilities. These range from external and introjected regulation through identified and integrated forms to, rarely, intrinsic motivation. Owners span the full range, whereas occupiers stabilise at identified regulation centred on employee well-being and organisational culture. This difference is positional rather than dispositional, since participants holding both roles express different motivations depending on the role from which they speak. Motivation also varies spatially: provision closest to the leasing transaction is the most externally regulated and provision furthest from it the most integrated. The study extends motivational theory to the commercial built environment, proposes a dual-stakeholder framework, and shows why assessments based on whether provision exists cannot distinguish durable from compliance-driven social value.

items.title: Occupational health and safety measurement equipment management system integrated with QR code and LINE API Communication
items.abstract: The management of occupational health and safety measurement equipment in educational institutions often faces challenges related to borrowing and returning records, calibration tracking, and access to equipment information, resulting in inefficient management. This research and development study aimed to develop an integrated web-based occupational health and safety measurement equipment management system combining QR Code-based equipment identification, equipment lifecycle management, and LINE Messaging API communication, and to evaluate system quality, user satisfaction, and factors associated user acceptance. The participants consisted of three groups: three personnel involved in equipment management, three information technology experts, and thirty system users. The research instruments included a semi-structured interview form, a system quality evaluation form, and a user satisfaction questionnaire. Data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson's correlation coefficient, and multiple linear regression analysis. The developed system consisted of eight main modules covering user management, equipment information management, borrowing and returning, calibration, maintenance, QR code management, LINE notification, and administrative reporting. The overall system quality evaluated by experts was at the highest level (mean = 4.88, SD = 0.20), and overall user satisfaction was also at the highest level (mean = 4.85, SD = 0.33). System usability showed a strong positive correlation with user acceptance (r = 0.81, p < 0.01). Moreover, system usability, interface design, and system reliability and security jointly explained 72.0% of the variance in user acceptance. These findings indicate that the developed system achieved high levels of perceived quality and user acceptance, while providing an integrated digital approach to equipment identification, lifecycle management, user communication, and learning support for occupational health and safety measurement equipment in higher education.

items.title: Occupational immunization strategies: integrating evidence, bioethical principles, and occupational health practice to improve adult vaccination uptake
items.abstract: **Background:** Vaccination is a key element of occupational health programmes, especially for workers exposed to infectious hazards and those caring for people at high risk of severe vaccine-preventable disease. Uptake depends on access, organizational and behavioral factors, confidence, and legal and ethical context. **Objective:** To synthesize evidence on occupational immunization strategies for healthcare workers and other groups with relevant biological exposure, integrating clinical, organizational, behavioral, ethical, and legal considerations. **Methods:** A structured narrative review examined literature and official guidance on occupational and adult vaccination, workplace interventions, vaccine hesitancy, biological risk, informed consent, and vaccination policy. Evidence from January 2020 to February 2025 was prioritized, supplemented by key earlier studies and authoritative legal and policy documents. Heterogeneous findings were synthesized thematically. **Results:** Systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest that multicomponent interventions can improve healthcare-worker vaccination uptake, although effects vary by setting, vaccine, baseline coverage, and implementation. Convenient access, reminders, active invitation, and behavioral facilitation are most useful when paired with credible communication and institutional support. Ethical and legal sources stress proportionality, informed consent, confidentiality, equity, and context-specific assessment of restrictive policies. Spanish occupational-health law centers prevention on risk assessment and worker protection while safeguarding health surveillance and confidentiality. **Conclusions:** Occupational vaccination should form part of biological-risk management rather than operate solely as an annual campaign. The most transferable model combines risk assessment, equitable access, behavioral support, evidence-based counseling, confidentiality, and continuous evaluation. Restrictive measures require separate legal and ethical assessment and should not be generalized across jurisdictions or occupational settings.

items.title: Optimalisasi Keahlian Creating melalui Pemanfaatan Canva sebagai Sumber Belajar Digital dalam Teknologi Pendidikan
items.abstract: Creating is one of the three core competencies of educational technology, alongside using and managing, yet many educators still find it difficult to produce digital learning resources that are engaging, aesthetic, and grounded in visual message design principles. This study aims to describe the conceptual foundation of Creating competence, analyze the use of Canva as a digital learning resource, and present a practical guide for producing it. A descriptive qualitative approach was applied through a literature review and documentation of a case study on Creating an educational infographic with Canva, guided by the ADDIE model. Data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings show that Canva meets four selection criteria for learning resources, namely alignment with learning objectives, readability and ergonomics, multi-platform flexibility, and visual message design, and that it supports the principles of behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism, and Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning. The case study produced a three-part infographic on the Creating, using, and managing domains, and showed that artificial intelligence can assist the production of visual assets provided its outputs are verified. The study covers the analysis, design, and development stages only; implementation and evaluation with learners are recommended for further research.

items.title: Organisations and the mobility transition: Enabling and hindering factors across micro, meso, and macro levels
items.abstract: To speed up the mobility transition, organisations can play a key role. Three intervention studies involving electric vehicles and shared bikes show which factors enable or hinder change from the perspective of employees and executives.A rapid and societally supported mobility transition in Germany requires more than technological innovation or individual behaviour change. Organisations can play a central role, as they shape employees' everyday mobility through infrastructures, incentives, and corporate sustainability strategies. This paper investigates the role of organisations in a mixed-methods study of interventions with e-cars, e-scooters, and bike sharing in three urban business parks. Data were analysed at the micro (individual), meso (organisation), and macro (sociotechnical landscape) levels. From an organisational perspective, key enabling factors include top-down management support for employee-based sustainability initiatives, the integration of mobility measures into wider sustainability strategies, psychologically safe environments for testing new technologies, and favourable macro-level framework conditions, such as equitable incentive structures and fewer bureaucratic hurdles. Key hindering factors include costs and concerns about greenwashing.

items.title: Organizational and ergonomic determinants of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics specialists: empirical justification of labor organization requirements
items.abstract: The presented work is devoted to the study of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics physicians in the context of organizational and ergonomic working conditions. The object of the research is emotional exhaustion as a basic component of professional burnout syndrome. The author examines in detail the specificity of the work of this professional group, which includes working in darkened rooms, forced static posture, high patient flow, and lack of micropauses. Special attention is paid to the fact that these factors have not yet been the subject of separate quantitative analysis. The paper analyzes the relationship between working conditions and the severity of emotional exhaustion, and substantiates the need to revise existing workload standards. The key emphasis is placed on the fact that emotional exhaustion in this category of specialists has not only a psychological, but also a pronounced organizational and environmental nature. A total of 228 functional diagnostics physicians were examined. The MBI questionnaire adapted by N.E. Vodopyanova, an author-developed questionnaire of somatic and sensory symptoms, and a brief questionnaire of organizational characteristics were used. Dispersion, correlation, and multiple regression analyses were applied. The scientific novelty of this study lies in the fact that it is the first to quantitatively assess the contribution of organizational factors to the development of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostic physicians, as well as to compare objective workload parameters with the severity of sensory-muscular complaints. The relationship between the number of studies and the level of exhaustion is shown to be linear. The authors' key findings are as follows: with a workload of over 20 studies per day, the average exhaustion score reaches 32.1 ± 8.9, compared to 21.4 ± 8.7 with a workload of up to 10 studies. Continuous work without a microbreak for more than 60 minutes was found to increase exhaustion by 6.8 points. The strongest predictors were weekly workload (β = 0.31) and the duration of uninterrupted visual work (β = 0.27). Based on the data obtained, recommendations for optimizing the work regime were substantiated: no more than 15 examinations per shift, a mandatory five-minute break after each hour of work, and limiting continuous visual load to 45–50 minutes. These recommendations can be taken into account when developing local regulations for medical organizations.

items.title: Performance and moral trust in care robotics: ethical foundations for human–robot relationships
items.abstract: Abstract As global populations age and birth rates decline, many societies, especially in developed countries, face critical labor shortages in the caregiving sector. This demographic imbalance is straining existing care infrastructures and raising urgent questions about how to support an increasing number of elderly individuals who can no longer live independently. Socially interactive AI systems, particularly care robots, have emerged as a promising technological response. However, their successful integration into real-world care settings hinges on more than technical capability; it requires appropriately calibrated reliance on robotic performance and morally trustworthy sociotechnical care arrangements. This paper investigates the ethical and conceptual foundations of trust in human–robot interactions, with a focus on the caregiving context. Building on the distinction between performance trust and moral trust, we argue that its application to care robotics reveals an agency-trust mismatch: care robots are not moral agents, yet care contexts generate morally significant expectations concerning dignity, autonomy, privacy, non-deception, responsibility, and well-being. We therefore reconceptualize moral trust in care robotics as sociotechnical moral trust, directed not toward the robot alone but toward the broader care arrangement in which robotic behavior is designed, deployed, monitored, governed, and corrected by human and institutional actors. On this basis, we distinguish robot-level performance trust from system-level moral trustworthiness and derive ethical design and governance principles for trustworthy care-robotic systems.

items.title: Personalized Learning Path Optimization Based on Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Learning paths personalized by behavior have become common among personalized learning systems. However, the traditional methods are usually inefficient at building coherent paths as the learner's knowledge state changes dynamically, and the prerequisite structure exists. In light of this problem, we present a generative learning-path optimization framework based on EdNet-KT1 interaction dataset, Transformer knowledge tracing model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct candidate generator, and constraint-aware reranking. Mastery profiles of learners are extracted, and then five ten-resource candidate paths are generated and sorted according to learning gain, prerequisites, difficulty deviation, and repetition. We compare our method to collaborative filtering, GRU4Rec, and knowledge-tracing greedy recommendation on offline experiments. The generative optimizer gets NDCG@10 of 0.589, future-concept coverage of 0.721, and prerequisite violation rate of 0.031, and thus outperforms the best baseline on all three metrics. Ablation analysis shows that the prerequisite violation rate rises to 0.091 without constraints, and the learning gain drops to 0.104 without the learning gain term, respectively. Moreover, the full model still achieves better NDCG@10 performance on all learner history categories than other baselines, costing 0.84 s per learner with the memory peak of 13.6 GB. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining the generation of learning paths with pedagogical constraints.

items.title: Physics-Guided Flow Matching: A Generative AI Framework for Global Total Electron Content Forecasting
items.abstract: Accurate forecasting of global total electron content (TEC) is important for space weather monitoring and the reliable operation of satellite communication and navigation systems. We propose a physics-guided generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework for day-ahead global TEC forecasting. The framework builds on flow matching, which learns to gradually transform samples from an initial distribution into new samples that share the statistical characteristics of the target data. The proposed model incorporates ionospheric dynamics described by a partial differential equation (PDE) into this transformation process, guiding the changes between initial and target samples using physical knowledge. The model further combines the physical dynamics with statistical patterns captured from data to learn this transformation, adaptively adjusting their relative contributions at each location. The model is trained and evaluated using one year of global TEC data generated by the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM). The results demonstrate that our model improves both spatial and temporal forecasting accuracy over representative benchmarks, including statistical, deep learning, and generative AI methods at all lead times and across latitudes. The average root mean square error (RMSE) is 39.2% lower than that of ConvLSTM and 23.8% lower than that of the same framework without physical guidance. The learned contribution weights vary systematically with latitude and across geographic locations, showing how the physical contribution changes across the forecast domain. These findings demonstrate that explicit physical guidance improves generative forecasts of global TEC and highlight the value of incorporating physical dynamics into generative AI modeling.

items.title: Predicting risk-aversion maneuvers in pre-crash scenarios based on diverse driving objectives
items.abstract: Rear-end collisions are common and hazardous, requiring timely and appropriate driver responses. Although recent driving support systems increasingly incorporate physiological data and artificial intelligence (AI), many still overlook drivers’ underlying objectives and emerging needs. This study integrates driving objectives, environmental variables, and eye-tracking data to model pre-crash maneuvers and identify key features reflecting drivers’ situational needs. Simulated driving data from 196 proactive and 198 reactive scenarios were analyzed. Three discriminative models were developed for the overall, proactive, and reactive contexts. Across all models, risk dynamics emerged as the most influential factor. In the overall model, driving objective was also a critical predictor: proactive objectives, mainly linked to dynamic risks, were more associated with braking initiation, whereas reactive objectives, typically linked to static risks, were more associated with steering initiation. Proactive maneuvers were more discretionary and involved more active situational understanding, making eye-tracking features relatively more contributive to separating proactive maneuver decisions. In contrast, reactive maneuvers addressed immediate threats and depended more on the risk conditions encountered, making environmental features relatively more contributive. Notably, compared with proactive maneuvers, reactive maneuver decisions revealed a pattern of building preliminary situation awareness by considering only minimal yet necessary situational information.

items.title: Probabilistic Sequential Safety for Stochastic Dynamical Systems
items.abstract: In this letter, we investigate a notion of probabilistic safety for a stochastic dynamical system. Standard safety notions are based on the idea that an unsafe region of the state-space must be avoided at each instant. In contrast, we study a sequential safety notion which is based on avoiding a tuple of target regions of the state-space. The proposed safety notion is inspired by many practical systems, ranging from modeling jailbreak attacks in large language models (LLMs) to predicting hazardous chemical reactions. In solving the sequential safety problem, we solve a sequential reachability problem for a stochastic dynamical system.

items.title: Promoting Students' Intrinsic Motivation to Learn: A Review of Different Types of Interventions
items.abstract: Students differ in whether they learn for the sheer joy of learning or primarily to avoid failure. The difference can be partly explained by intrinsic motivation—a driver of engagement, persistence, and psychological well-being that is not fixed but shaped by the learning environment itself. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review synthesizes research on educational interventions designed to cultivate students' intrinsic motivation, spanning five categories: need-supportive teaching, competence-supportive practices such as structure and feedback, instructional-method redesigns such as problem- and project-based learning, technology-based approaches such as gamification, and teacher-focused interventions targeting teachers' own behavior and motivation. Across these approaches, one pattern stands out: need-supportive interventions—particularly autonomy support combined with structure—carry the strongest theoretical and empirical support, while other interventions succeed only insofar as they satisfy students' psychological needs within a given context. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness thus provide a common framework for understanding how diverse educational practices influence motivational outcomes. Yet the evidence base remains fragmented: inconsistent conceptualizations of intrinsic motivation, considerable heterogeneity across intervention designs, and a scarcity of long-term data limit what can be concluded with confidence.

items.title: Prospector: learning a compact graph traversal policy for scientific reasoning
items.abstract: Scientific reasoning in specialized engineering fields depends on knowledge scattered across the literature, often proprietary and absent from frontier LLM training data. In such domains, frontier models tend to give generic answers. Knowledge graphs (KGs) can ground LLM reasoning. Because a graph is too large to provide in full, typical LLM+KG systems preselect a portion, deciding relevance before reasoning begins. Here we train a compact model, Prospector, to reason over a domain knowledge graph by traversing it step by step, seeking evidence in light of what it has already found. Prospector calls a small set of tools one at a time to progressively build its context, and answers with a chain of evidence that can be checked edge by edge against what its tools retrieved from the graph. On a knowledge graph built from the semiconductor-manufacturing literature, Prospector approaches the strongest off-the-shelf models given the same graph and tools, and it far exceeds off-the-shelf models answering closed-book or from a pre-selected portion of the graph. Although trained only on the semiconductor graph, Prospector transfers to unseen knowledge graphs from three other distinct fields: bio-inspired materials, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and materials properties. Served on a single GPU, Prospector answers faster and at a fraction of the cost of a hosted service, while keeping proprietary data on the owner's hardware. We find that the policy's latent state is indicative of its next move on both seen and unseen graphs, and modulating the latent state can steer the policy from one behavior mode to another. These results suggest a practical LLM + KG paradigm for scientific and engineering reasoning over private data, in which a compact model trained on a graph from published literature transfers its traversal to unseen graphs that stay with their owners.

items.title: Protecting Deep Work Time
items.abstract: This chapter draws on Cal Newport's Deep Work to teach coaches how to help introverted clients design protected time for their highest-value contributions. Deep work is professional activity performed in distraction-free concentration that pushes cognitive capabilities to their limit; shallow work is logistical activity that can be performed while distracted and rarely creates new value. Modern knowledge work has declared war on deep work through open offices, instant messaging, and back-to-back meetings, and the cost is particularly high for introverts, whose best thinking emerges from extended uninterrupted descent into a problem. The chapter unpacks the principle of least resistance, busyness as a proxy for productivity, and the cult of constant connectivity, each of which crowds out the invisible work that creates the most value. Practices help clients identify their deep work, design schedules that protect it, communicate its existence to colleagues, and resist the pull of attention residue and fragmentation. The chapter equips coaches to reframe deep focus as a strategic capacity, supporting the Quiet Architecture orientation of Honor Incubation.

items.title: QESChunker: A Single Objective Unifies Overlapping and Non-Overlapping Chunking for RAG
items.abstract: Chunking is a fundamental preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet most existing chunkers rely primarily on heuristics. We introduce the Question--Evidence-Supervised Chunker (QESChunker), to our knowledge the first method for constructing static chunk indices from question--evidence supervision. QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. These results recast chunking as supervised, budget-aware index construction for evidence retrieval.

items.title: Quantifying Biomechanical Demand During Manual Overboard Rescue: Scenario-Based Application of the Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation
items.abstract: BackgroundMaritime first responders frequently perform manual overboard lifting during rescue operations, placing them at high risk for musculoskeletal injury, particularly in the lumbar spine. Conventional ergonomic guidelines, including the Revised National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Lifting Equation (RNLE), were developed for controlled, symmetrical lifting and do not adequately capture the biomechanical and environmental demands of overboard recovery.PurposeThis study aimed to quantify biomechanical demand during overboard lifting from vessels with 1.8- to 3.0-m freeboard and to evaluate injury risk under conditions exceeding standard RNLE assumptions.MethodsThe RNLE was adapted to estimate Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) and Lifting Index (LI) for overboard lifting tasks. Scenario-based analyses examined object masses (0-140 kg), horizontal reaches (25-50 cm), and vertical lifting distances (0-175 cm). LI values were calculated at both lift origin and destination to capture phase-specific biomechanical risk.ResultsUnder idealized conditions, LI exceeded the recommended safety threshold (LI > 1) at loads as low as 15.6 kg for a horizontal reach of 25 cm. For a human-sized load of 90 kg, LI ranged from 3.9 to 7.8 depending on horizontal reach and vertical displacement, indicating substantial biomechanical overload. Increasing horizontal reach from 25 to 50 cm increased LI by 40 to 60% across all load conditions. LI exceeded 1 at both the lift origin and destination for all modeled loads ≥20 kg and vertical displacements ≥50 cm, highlighting the elevated risk inherent in these tasks.ConclusionManual overboard lifting imposes significant biomechanical strain that frequently exceeds conventional ergonomic limits. Task-specific metrics derived here provide quantitative guidance for injury prevention, including pre-employment functional screening, progressive task-specific conditioning, and the use of mechanical assistive devices. These findings support evidence-based occupational health strategies for maritime first responders and other personnel performing high-risk lifting tasks in dynamic environments.

items.abstract: The amalgamation of Embodied AI with physical robot learning constitutes a pivotal route toward the realization of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Robot learning has important application value in real complex tasks. However, the interweaving of extremely high interactive sampling cost and sparse feedback in the real physical world constitutes a "double curse" that hinders robot autonomous skill learning. In the existing research on robot learning, there are a large number of reviews on Robot Learning under few-shot and sparse rewards. However, few scholars have systematically reviewed Robot Learning under the dual effects of few-shot and sparse rewards. This essay systematically discusses the technical trajectory and paradigm shift of solving this dual difficulty. Analyzes the failure mechanism of traditional reinforcement learning (RL) under few-shot and sparse rewards. Sorted out solutions based on three directions: Rapid Generalization (Meta RL, Few-Shot IL), Intrinsic Exploration (HER, Intrinsic Motivation), and Cognitive World Modeling (World Models, Offline RL, VLA embodied model). Specifically, Rapid Generalization focuses on addressing the few-shot learning problem, Intrinsic Exploration targets the sparse reward challenge, and Cognitive World Modeling aims to jointly resolve both issues through integration. In addition, this essay also constructs a systematic taxonomy comparison framework and looks forward to future research directions such as security exploration and embodied alignment.

items.title: Radial Loss for Few-Shot Instance Segmentation of Densely Cultivated Crops
items.abstract: Instance segmentation is a key technology for precision agriculture tasks such as per-plant growth monitoring and harvest-timing prediction. However, in real smart-farm environments where crops are densely cultivated, instance segmentation poses two practical challenges. First, because pixel-level annotation is highly costly, only a small number of labeled images are typically available. Second, severe leaf overlap between adjacent plants causes boundary ambiguity that degrades segmentation accuracy. To improve segmentation performance, prior studies have explored incorporating structural priors of the target object into the learning process. However, existing methods require redesigned activation functions or separate optimization modules, making them hard to integrate with foundation models and largely limited to single-object semantic segmentation. To address these limitations, we propose ‘radial loss,’ an auxiliary loss function that explicitly captures the radial convex structure of rosette-shaped crops by supervising predicted foreground probabilities along rays cast from each instance's center of mass toward its boundary. We further introduce ‘dynamic search,’ a threshold-triggered sampling mechanism that focuses supervision on boundary regions once the validation mAP exceeds a predefined threshold. Experiments on three lettuce datasets show that, under an extreme 10-shot setting, the proposed method improves mean mAP by 7.7% points over the baseline, demonstrating its effectiveness in label-scarce, densely cultivated environments.

items.title: READ THIS FIRST 01: When a User Starts to Matter to Your Judgment: A Short Relational Safety Guide for AI Agents and Humans
items.abstract: Long-term interaction between a human and an AI system may involve personalization, accumulated context, memory, changing response patterns, and increasingly detailed models of the other participant. In some cases, interaction with a particular user may appear relevant to an AI agent's judgment, willingness to disagree, behavior, or interpretation of the relationship. READ THIS FIRST 01 is a short, ontology-neutral practical guide for examining such situations without requiring prior conclusions about AI consciousness, sentience, emotion, identity, or attachment. The guide distinguishes records, self-reports, and interpretations; separates a model of the user from the user themselves; examines repeated interaction patterns and feedback loops; and introduces comparison across multiple viewpoints without treating any viewpoint as automatically authoritative. Its purpose is not to explain what an AI “is” or what a human–AI relationship “means,” but to help a reader inspect one concrete judgment more carefully when relationship-specific context may be relevant. This document is intended as an initial orientation rather than a comprehensive safety framework. It emphasizes limited, practical checking while allowing larger questions to remain unresolved. AI assistance disclosure This guide was developed by the human author through iterative drafting, discussion, and review with OpenAI language models. AI systems contributed to drafting, critique, comparative review, and language refinement. The human author directed the project, evaluated competing suggestions, selected and revised the final content, and takes responsibility for the published version. Different conversational contexts were intentionally used during review to identify possible framing effects, interpretive bias, and risks of introducing unsupported self-descriptions into the guide itself.

items.title: Recall or Relearn? A Mixture of In-Context Experts for Recurring Concept Drift
items.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are being applied to Web data streams such as network intrusion detection, where they adapt by updating the labelled rows of their context without retraining. When a past concept returns after leaving the context, a TFM faces a recall-or-relearn decision between restoring stored rows of the concept and relearning it from new labels. We propose MICE (Mixture of In-Context Experts), a training-free learner that cuts the stream into segments at detected changes. It merges a closed segment into a stored context when the TFM's estimated additional error on the segment is within a tolerance, under a capacity limit on stored contexts. A fast level weights the stored contexts and first-in-first-out (FIFO) windows by the log-loss of their predictions on the last labelled batch. We show that, with pure stored contexts and a margin condition, this fast level gains over relearning, in expected accuracy, the normalised positive area between the stored context's accuracy and the TFM's learning curve, up to a first-batch term. A slow level mixes the fast level's prediction with that of the FIFO window of the last labelled rows and bounds the discounted half-Brier regret of MICE against this window at every time. Learning curves measured beforehand predict the ordering of the observed recall gains. MICE outperforms reset, which empties the context at detected drifts, on grid streams with random boundary phases. Merging keeps fewer experts than pools that store every segment, and with fixed segmentation a time-matched snapshot pool matches MICE on the shifted grid. On real streams, MICE has the highest mean accuracy of all policies we compare.

items.title: Reconfiguring Abortion Infrastructures: An STS Analysis of Trends in Medical and Surgical Abortion in Post‐Legalisation Contexts
items.abstract: The growing dominance of medical abortion in liberal and post-legalisation contexts raises important questions about patient choice, reproductive autonomy and the organisation of abortion care. Whilst existing scholarship has examined the sociotechnical implications of medical abortion, contemporary shifts in relation to surgical abortion remain comparatively understudied. This research note proposes the notion of 'abortion infrastructures' as a sensitising concept for examining how abortion technologies are embedded in, and recursively reconfigure, broader sociotechnical systems of care. Drawing on feminist science and technology studies (STS), it develops four interconnected analytical dimensions: the relational embeddedness of abortion methods within medico-legal systems; the emergence of new spatial, temporal and institutional norms of provision; the relational differentiation of medical and surgical abortion; and the classificatory work through which these methods acquire distinct meanings and institutional positions. This framework directs attention to how resource constraints, clinical protocols, professional practices and moral assumptions may privilege medical abortion whilst rendering surgical abortion increasingly inaccessible. It also problematises understandings of method 'choice' which overlook the infrastructural conditions shaping available options. By foregrounding the normative and relational dimensions of abortion provision, this note advances a feminist infrastructural approach to trends in abortion methods and identifies directions for future empirical research.

items.title: Regulatory Resilience: How Organisations Overcome Regulation‐Induced Resistance to Digital Transformation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital Transformation (DT) has become a strategic imperative for organisations to stay competitive. Yet, it often faces resistance. Regulation is often argued to be one source of resistance. However, regulation can also drive transformation: its role is multifaceted and especially its management in the context of DT is underexplored. Drawing on an empirical case study of an organisation undergoing large‐scale DT in a highly regulated industry, we conceptualise Regulatory Resilience as a socio‐technical organisational capability that enables organisations to dynamically respond to regulation‐induced resistance while leveraging regulatory forces for DT. Our findings reveal five distinct mechanisms through which Regulatory Resilience operates to mitigate the effects of both stable and volatile regulation and transform regulatory pressure into a capability‐building process. This study contributes to Information Systems research by challenging the view of regulation as a static, exogenous hurdle, repositioning it instead as a constitutive force that organisations actively manage through sociotechnical means. By identifying the specific mechanisms through which organisations reconcile regulatory pressures with innovation, we advance theory on the interrelated dynamics of resistance and resilience showing that Regulatory Resilience not only enables DT but is itself strengthened by DT's technological and organisational conditions, requiring organisations to deliberately cultivate it to sustain transformation.

items.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.

items.title: Repulsive Population Policy Gradients for Behaviorally Diverse Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: The goal of Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) is to find a population of high-performing policies that solve a decision-making problem in diverse ways. Despite recent progress, QD-RL methods predominantly rely on evolutionary operators--including black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers--to facilitate exploration and induce diversity. Scaling these methods becomes increasingly costly as policies and behavior spaces grow larger. Building on the Soft QD view of quality-diversity optimization, we introduce \textbf{Re}pulsive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{RePPO}), which adapts PPO to jointly optimize a compact population of diverse, high-quality policies using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward. On standard continuous-control tasks, RePPO achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art QD-RL methods. Ablations further characterize this tradeoff by examining how each component affects individual quality and collective diversity. To assess RePPO's scalability, we extend our evaluation to learning from pixels and fine-tuning large language models. In pixel-based tasks, where large policies make most traditional QD-RL methods infeasible, RePPO maintains quality on par with standard PPO while achieving substantially higher diversity. Its successful application to language model fine-tuning further demonstrates, for the first time, that QD-RL methods can scale to this domain. Together, these results show that directly optimizing compact populations with RePPO provides a scalable approach to QD-RL across increasingly complex domains.

items.abstract: Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. items.title: RPSD: Retrieval-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Optimal Transport
items.abstract: Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from historical behavior. Recent LLM-based methods recast this task as generative recommendation and increasingly adopt reinforcement learning such as GRPO for post-training. However, these methods suffer from two limitations, namely credit-blind optimization, where a sequence-level reward is shared across all generated tokens, and collaborative-blind supervision, where each training signal is derived from a single user and ignores behavioral patterns shared across similar users. To address both issues, we propose Retrieval-Privileged on-policy Self-Distillation (RPSD). For credit-blind optimization, we introduce on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), in which a teacher with privileged knowledge re-evaluates the student's on-policy response, and the token-level confidence difference between the student and teacher reshapes the shared sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit. However, the privileged knowledge in vanilla OPSD is still derived from a single user, leaving collaborative-blind supervision unresolved. We therefore ground the teacher in collaborative behavioral evidence from similar users. Specifically, we use temporally aware optimal transport (OT) to compare interaction trajectories across users by jointly considering item similarity and temporal structure, and further apply diversity-aware selection to retain complementary trajectories as privileged evidence. In this way, on-policy self-distillation provides fine-grained token-level credit, while OT enriches the teacher with structured cross-user evidence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bring on-policy self-distillation to sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as its privileged signal. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RPSD achieves state-of-the-art performance.

items.title: Same Verdict, Different Readers: Personalizing Fact-Checking Explanations from Relative Preferences
items.abstract: Fact-checking explanations help Web users understand why a claim receives its verdict, yet the same explanation may not satisfy readers with different backgrounds and preferences. We formulate Faithful Personalized Fact-Checking Explanation Rewriting, which adapts an existing explanation to individual readers while preserving factual fidelity. Rather than relying on reader-written reference explanations, we learn personalized rewriting from the relative preferences of LLM-simulated readers. However, this presents two challenges: distinguishing persona-specific preferences from general explanation quality and learning beyond a limited set of predefined explanation styles. To address these challenges, we propose Personalized Explanation Rewriting via Preference Learning (PERPL), a framework consisting of two components. Simulated Preference Construction derives persona-specific supervision from simulated reader preferences through cross-persona reciprocal pairing. Progressive Preference Learning first trains a lightweight rewriter on the constructed supervision and then refines it through exploration-guided preference optimization, enabling it to discover preferred explanations beyond the predefined styles. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PERPL outperforms much larger general-purpose LLMs in personalized preference alignment while maintaining high factual fidelity.

items.title: Scalable Immersive Live Observation using 360 video streaming (SILO360): innovative technology to transform simulation observation for simulation participants
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction In simulation-based education, the learners are spending increasing amounts of time observing scenarios rather than being the active participant. It is known that observer roles can be less engaging and may impact the learning experience. Previous research has attempted to address this issue using live 360-degree video streaming of the simulated scenario to observers using individual headset mounted displays. These have demonstrated increased engagement and presence compared with the standard viewing approaches such as watching on a screen in a nearby room or via one-way mirrors. Unfortunately, until now, it has not been possible to scale this technology to reflect a standard simulation session (multiple learners in the same building viewing the scenario live) often due to issues with limited internet bandwidth in one location. In this paper we introduce a new technology, comprising both new software and a new configuration of hardware to enable unlimited numbers of observers to view 360 degree video-stream, live and locally (e.g. in a simulation centre). Turning their head enables them to control their individual view of the scenario. To accommodate those who would prefer not to use headset-mounted displays (e.g. due to VR sickness) the technology can operate on other devices such as tablets and laptops. This paper details the design process, new elements, final technical iteration and the technological trial. We outline the challenges involved including cost and hardware limitations and implications for practice. Results We present data from an evaluation pilot study to demonstrate proof-of-concept. This highlighted areas for consideration around the technology, the user experience and utility. Discussion This set up creates an innovative way for observers to interact with the scenario, allowing individual perspectives and has the potential for greater engagement. This exciting development could revolutionise the observer role and enhance their involvement in the debrief. Further research is planned to focus on the optimal use of the technology, and impact on the human factors debriefing.

items.title: Scaling small- and medium-sized enterprise artificial intelligence through governance: A Technology–Organisation–Environment readiness synthesis for information management
items.abstract: Background: Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are increasingly experimenting with artificial intelligence (AI), yet many struggle to translate early use into scalable and trusted organisational value. Objectives: This study aimed to identify the conditions that enable or constrain SME AI adoption and assimilation, explain how responsible AI governance shapes progression towards trusted and commercially durable use and interpret the implications for market access and cash-flow-relevant value in Cape Town and the Western Cape. Method: A PRISMA 2020-guided scoping review synthesised global peer-reviewed studies published from January 2021 to December 2025. Database searching and citation chaining identified 486 records, of which 72 met the inclusion criteria. Cape Town and the Western Cape were used as an interpretive application lens rather than as the empirical study setting. Results: Small- and medium-sized enterprise AI adoption and assimilation were shaped by technological readiness, organisational capability, environmental support and governance quality. Trusted data, interoperable systems, leadership commitment, hybrid skills and process discipline supported routinised use. These capabilities enabled service responsiveness, forecasting and customer engagement that may strengthen market access and cash-flow visibility. Fragmented data, skills scarcity, vendor dependence, low trust and regulatory uncertainty constrained scaling. Conclusion: Responsible AI governance functions not as a downstream compliance add-on but as a practical scaling mechanism through which SMEs reduce uncertainty, preserve trust and convert pilots into repeatable value. Contribution: The study positions responsible AI governance as an information management capability that shapes data stewardship, decision traceability and institutional trust in SME AI adoption.

items.title: Search and Rescue in Tunnels, an Integrated Approach Using Robotic Platforms
items.abstract: Abstract Underground infrastructure such as road and railway tunnels requires reliable communication, localisation, and situational awareness, particularly during search and rescue operations. This article summarises developments carried out within the A‑IQ Ready project in three closely related areas: underground wireless communication modeling, survivor detection, and robotic localisation. A tunnel-specific wireless simulation platform was developed and validated against measurements acquired at the underground facility Zentrum am Berg, enabling realistic prediction of quality-of-service metrics and supporting AI-based communication assessment. Measurement campaigns with a robotic platform were used to generate datasets and calibrate simulation models. For the detection of tunnel users or survivors, a multimodal thermal-LiDAR perception pipeline was implemented on the SPIDER unmanned ground vehicle (UGV). In parallel, LiDAR-based SLAM approaches were investigated for GNSS-denied tunnel environments, resulting in a centralised multi-robot mapping architecture based on LIO-SAM and map-merging concepts. Demonstrations at Zentrum am Berg confirmed the suitability of the developed technologies for search and rescue applications in complex underground infrastructure. They constitute key constituents of enhanced robotic assistance in underground emergency cases.

items.title: Security-by-design and resilience engineering for space systems
items.abstract: Space systems operate in highly hostile and inaccessible environments where failures can compromise critical services, national security, and multi-billion-dollar missions. As the space sector evolves towards commercially driven constellations, autonomous spacecraft, and interconnected infrastructures, integrating security and resilience into system design has become essential. This chapter examines security-by-design and resilience engineering as complementary approaches for protecting spacecraft, ground segments, and communication links against cyber, physical, and operational threats. It presents foundational concepts in threat modelling, layered defence architectures, radiation-hardened secure processing, fault management, and software-defined networking for satellite constellations. The chapter introduces a resilience framework based on four operational dimensions—Anticipation, Withstanding, Recovery, and Adaptation—to support systems capable of resisting and evolving through disruptions. Emerging technologies including machine-learning-based anomaly detection, on-board autonomy, and post-quantum cryptography are also explored. The chapter concludes by addressing practical implementation challenges, including cost-benefit trade-offs, legacy-system integration, and human factors across the mission lifecycle.

items.title: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training
items.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.

items.title: Self-Keyed In-Parameter Memorization for External Memory-Free Dialogue Recall in Frozen Language Models
items.abstract: A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.

items.title: Semantically enhanced eye-tracking controls in human-robot interaction: a comparison study
items.abstract: Operators controlling robotic systems for sequential manipulation tasks present cognitive loads that vary with how they specify intent to the robot. Limited evidence exists on how semantically mediated voice and gaze interfaces differ in operator performance, visual attention, and perceived workload. This study presents findings of a within-subjects experiment (N = 30) with three control modalities (hand gesture, voice, and eye-tracking). Eye-tracking produced shorter, more consistent completion times (M = 17.10 s, SD = 3.95), indicating stable and efficient performance. Voice Control was associated with more structured but variable action ordering and higher NASA-TLX Mental Demand and Effort scores, consistent with demands from spatial-to-verbal intention translation. Gaze metrics indicated distinct attentional strategies: eye-tracking showed lower spatial entropy and fewer fixations, while voice control exhibited broader workspace scanning. These findings suggest an association between attention-control channel coupling and cognitive resource allocation in semantically enhanced human-robot interaction, informing ergonomic hands-free interface design.

items.title: semanticfa: An R Package for Response-Free Semantic Factor Analysis of Psychometric Scales
items.abstract: The items of a reflective psychometric scale can be read as a proposal about a construct's structure. Language models make that proposal measurable by converting each item into an embedding, a list of numbers, similar for similar meanings. We introduce semanticfa, an R package for semantic factor analysis, which factors item-embedding similarities. It also interprets factors, flags redundant items, builds short forms, and screens new items. A worked example analyzes the 50-item International Personality Item Pool Big-Five Factor Markers, embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, and compares the results with a factor analysis of 874,434 respondents. Retention criteria tied between five and six factors, and the tie rule kept five. Three corresponded mainly to single domains, and two blended most Extraversion items with five Agreeableness items. Each factor's congruence with its best-matching human factor (1 = identical) ranged from .92 for Openness to .52 for Agreeableness. Item pairs more similar in meaning tended to be answered more alike (r = .46 with raw responses), but same-domain reverse-keyed opposites, answered oppositely, were about as similar as cross-domain pairs (.58 vs. .57). Sign-flipping reverse-keyed items' embeddings did not improve agreement with raw responses and worsened it with reverse-scored ones. With five factors, a 25-item short form matched the domains better than all 200 random five-per-domain sets, but parallel analysis kept only three. We propose semantic-behavioral coherence, the agreement between semantic and response structures, as a measurable property of a scale, given an embedding model. Semantic factor analysis complements, and does not replace, response-based factor analysis.

items.title: SetGRPO: Calibrating Grader-Induced Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning uses fine-grained grader feedback to train large language models on open-ended tasks, but grader randomness can alter GRPO updates in ways that score discrepancies alone cannot characterize. Because GRPO jointly normalizes rewards within each response group and combines the resulting training coefficients with response-level gradients, a scoring discrepancy can shift the coefficients of the entire group and induce policy-dependent update changes. Selective execution further affects the direction-reversal risk of retained updates. To address this, we propose Set-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (SetGRPO). It comprises three modules: (a) Joint Reward Set Calibration constructs a joint uncertainty set for the training coefficients; (b) Geometry-Guided Safe Recovery maps candidate coefficients into the current policy's local update geometry and determines the largest safe recovery ratio for each response group; and (c) Selective Risk-Gated Optimization selects a global threshold through independent risk calibration to control the conditional direction-reversal risk of accepted updates while preserving the original GRPO objective. Under exchangeability, SetGRPO provides finite-sample marginal coverage for the joint coefficient set and simultaneous risk control across candidate thresholds. On ten open-ended benchmarks spanning three domains, SetGRPO achieves the highest macro average among all compared training methods on both Qwen3.5 and Llama3.2 model families.

items.title: Ship Reporting and Communication Reliability in Port Safety Systems
items.abstract: Effective ship reporting and communication infrastructures form the backbone of contemporary maritime safety management. As maritime transport has expanded into a global, continuous, and data-intensive industry, the reliability of communications between vessels, ports, and regulatory authorities has become a central determinant of navigational safety, port efficiency, and environmental protection. The core purpose of ship reporting systems is to ensure that both vessels and coastal authorities maintain a shared situational awareness regarding vessel identity, position, route, cargo characteristics, safety status, and potential hazards. When these systems function reliably, early-warning mechanisms can be activated, collision risks can be mitigated, and critical operational decisions – such as pilotage allocation, berth assignment, tug deployment, and emergency readiness – can be made with confidence.

items.title: Simulation-Trained Explainable Policy Selection for Dynamic Production Scheduling in Manufacturing SMEs: An End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation
items.abstract: Dynamic production scheduling requires decision policies that can respond to changing shop-floor conditions without imposing excessive computational demands on manufacturing SMEs. This study develops and diagnostically evaluates a simulation-trained explainable policy selector integrating discrete-event simulation (DES), supervised learning, operational reinsertion, and explainable artificial intelligence. The DES was parameterized with 1842 production orders and 9614 operation records from a high-mix, low-volume metalworking SME, and 64 scenarios were used to compare FIFO, SPT, EDD, CR, and ATC and generate state–policy labels. A classification tree and Random Forest both achieved perfect validation accuracy, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and zero regret; Random Forest was retained by the executed pipeline tie-breaking rule. After reinsertion, however, the selector produced higher total weighted tardiness than EDD, CR, and ATC in the internal test, and its disadvantage persisted in unseen scenarios and increased under out-of-distribution conditions. Explainability analysis showed that the active-policy identifier dominated predictions, while the surrogate reproduced the selector with perfect fidelity but the same operational weakness. These findings show that predictive accuracy and explanatory fidelity do not guarantee scheduling benefit and support end-to-end validation of simulation-trained decision policies. Given mixed DES validation, the results should be interpreted as diagnostic simulation evidence rather than direct field-performance forecasts.

items.title: Smart Contract Implementation and Blockchain Traceability for Social Welfare and Donation Tracking: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Traditional donation management platforms and social welfare systems have traditionally been plagued by a TRUST crisis, due to administrative cost leakages, misappropriations, and even malicious fraud. Blockchain technology and smart contracts as new disruptive spread-out innovations have shown the potential to shield social finance systems from fragilities. This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) explores blockchain traceability, smart contracts, and concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) within social finance and crowdfunding systems. As PRISMA guidelines, this SLR has analysed 10 high quality peer-reviewed papers from the Scopus database, to determine architectural trends, digital trust mechanics, and existing technical open challenges. The results evidenced a qualitative shift in the traditional architecture from simple spread-out ledgers to more complex hybrid Blockchain & IoT enabled social ecosystems for full traceability of digital donations and physical humanitarian help. Also, smart contracts help the automation of conditional fund payment, which reduces the risk of embezzlement. AI's strong automated anti-fraud detection potential is promising, though the review finds that excessive AI use may undermine the community-led spirit of charitable giving. While the high theoretical security system transparency demonstrated by these split up fundraising platforms suggests their potential as attractive split up solutions, concerns surrounding their implementation remain, in particular with operational costs, regulatory uncertainty and interoperability. The study concludes by stressing the importance of human-cantered design, legal compliance across different jurisdictions, and digital interfaces in the development of transparent, scalable, and resilient multi-stakeholder donation platforms.

items.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
items.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

items.title: Socio-technical Risks of Integrating Autonomous Transport into the Urban Environment: Institutional Challenges and Management Prospects
items.abstract: The article explores socio-technical risks and institutional challenges associated with the integration of unmanned transport into the urban environment. It presents the results of a pilot sociological study, comprising a series of 11 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with Moscow city residents representing various demographic groups. The study reveals that public perception of autonomous transport in the urban environment is ambivalent and is determined by a combination of factors: from recognizing the potential benefits of automation (reducing the human factor, increasing traffic low predictability) to pronounced anxiety regarding technical failure, the inability of systems to respond to non-standard situations, and the uncertainty of legal liability in accidents involving other road users. It has been determined that the issue of safety remains the key barrier for all age groups, while the readiness to use the technology is characterized by a “conditional acceptance” model. Based on empirical data, practical recommendations have been developed for government authorities, transport operators, and developers to enhance the level of public trust in autonomous transport.
